question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

payload.holding: The High Court modified the compensation amounts awarded in the connected claim cases (partly enhancing some and upholding others) and granted pay-and-recover rights to the insurance company upon finding a breach of policy conditions due to the lack of a special endorsement on the driver's license for transporting hazardous goods.
payload.ratio: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license as prescribed under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach of insurance policy terms entitling the insurer to pay and recover.

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.court: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Madhugiri
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

payload.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
payload.court: Supreme Court of India
payload.holding: The Supreme Court held that the principles laid down in Swaran Singh's case regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims, and that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
payload.ratio: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between the insurer and the insured where no third party is involved.

In all these cases identical questions are involved and therefore the appeals are disposed of by this
common judgment.
In each of the impugned judgments the concerned High Court held that the principles laid down by
this Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004 (3) SCC
297) is applicable even to claims other than third party claims. Some of these appeals also relate to
orders passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi (in short the
'Commission') where a similar view has been taken.
Since there has been elaborate analysis of the factual position it would be appropriate to decide the
basic principles in law and ask the High Courts/Commissions to decide the cases afresh keeping in
mind the view expressed in the present judgment.
The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) applied to claims which involved only the insurance
company and the owner of the vehicle i.e. where there was no third party involved. It has been
highlighted by learned counsel for the appellants that Swaran Singh's case (supra) was rendered in
the background of Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (in short the 'Act') which has no
application to cases where there is no third party involved.
In response, learned counsel appearing for the respondents have submitted that there can be no
difference of approach in cases where the dispute relates to the claim relating to the insurer and the
insured.

stees v. Southern Union General Insurance Co. of Australasia Ltd.
(1928 Ch 793) the Chancery Division noted the plight of the third party victims and observed as
follows:
"As it seems to me it does not differ substantially from the position in In re
Harrington Motor Co.
In giving judgment Atkin L.J. said that he thought that the appellant had a real
grievance; but the general rule of law was too strong to allow the Court to make any
exception, however the Court might sympathize with the appellant. The position in
law was quite clear, and it was that the appellant had no right or claim against the
insurance company or against money paid by the insurance company. The assured
had a direct right of recourse against the insurance company, but a third party had no
such right, because there was no privity between him and the insurance company,
and it was difficult to see how a special right could be said to exist against the
insurance company, or any right to claim money paid over by the insurance company,
merely because the assured happened to be in financial difficulties.
Upon what grounds of equity or legal logic can it be argued that, because the law, on
grounds of public policy, compels the creditor, the liability to whom is the event upon
which the right of a bankrupt or of an insolvent company to payment of the sum
covered by the contract arises, to be content with such share of the assets of the
bankrupt or the company in liquidation as a pari passu distribution between creditors
will give, these assets are not to include the payment due under the contract? "That
seems to me," said Atkin L.J., "to be a direct statement by the learned Lord Justice;
indeed a statement of the law that the third party is compelled by the law to be
content with such a share of the assets as a pari passu distribution between the
creditors will give.
Now so far as this case is concerned everything which has been said applies here.

. V.
National Insurance Company Ltd. and Ors. (2005 (9) SCC 174).
The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a
valid driving license. In Swaran Singh's case (supra) the following situations were noted:
(i) the driver had a license but it was fake;

(ii) the driver had no license at all;
(iii) the driver originally had a valid license but it had expired as on the date of the
accident and had not been renewed;
(iv) the license was for a class of vehicles other than that which was the insured
vehicle;
(v) the license was a learner's license.
Category (i) may cover two types of situations. First, the license itself was fake and the second is
where originally that license is fake but there has been a renewal subsequently in accordance with
law.
Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor
vehicles.
Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these
are cases where there is no third party involved.
According to learned counsel for the appellants, in such cases the logic i.e. let the insurer pay and
recover from the insured company does not apply.
As noted above, there is no contractual relation between the third party and the insurer. Because of
the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.

payload.court: High Court Of Judicature At Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
payload.holding: The appeal of the insurance company is dismissed, and the appeal of the claimants is partly allowed by setting aside the finding of contributory negligence, factoring in future prospects, and enhancing the total compensation to Rs. 13,74,876/- with a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan that does not conclusively indicate a head-on collision. Furthermore, even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). The accident involved a commercial truck whose driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting and adverse precedents and strategy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: third-party death claim, insurer raised defence of invalid driving licence. The court held the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It establishes that even where the insurer proves a breach (invalid licence), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment. The insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner, not refusal to pay the claimant.
supporting.quote: the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Pursuant to Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision of Karnataka High Court directly holding that even a fundamental breach of policy conditions does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively analyses the statutory scheme. It rejects the argument that a 'fundamental breach' allows the insurer to walk away from third-party liability. The only exception is fraud/collusion, which is not present here.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... or a policy covering other risks

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Most factually analogous: the driver had NO driving licence at all (not expired, not wrong class). The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus. The driver genuinely had no licence. Despite that, the tribunal applied pay-and-recover. It directly refutes the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability to anyone.'
supporting.quote: it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle in the manner provided under law.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (heavy goods vehicle) where driver had LMV licence but no endorsement for HGV. The court applied pay-and-recover. The principle extends to our case where the driver had no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the commercial nature of the vehicle does not change the pay-and-recover principle. The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be contracted away.
supporting.quote: the insurer would remain liable to the innocent third party, but it may be able to recover from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required, there is a breach but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial/transport vehicle, driver lacked proper licence class. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that licence deficiency does not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming that even for transport/commercial vehicles, the pay-and-recover principle applies. The insurer cannot refuse to pay the third party.
supporting.quote: the Insurance Company must first pay the compensation amount to the claimant and then recover the same from the insured owner due to breach of policy conditions regarding the driver's license.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle while possessing a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 overrides policy conditions about licence endorsements.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court precedent that the insurer's obligation to third parties is statutory and cannot be defeated by technical licence deficiencies. While this case involved a driver who had some licence (unlike our facts), the ratio on the primacy of third-party protection is binding.
supporting.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case where the court held the insurer must pay the third party. The ratio extends to any licence deficiency.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the licence is not valid on the date of accident, the third-party claim is not defeated. The insurer's remedy is against the insured.
supporting.quote: the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover, but the third party must still be paid.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (tanker) where driver lacked special endorsement for hazardous goods. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that third-party claims are not defeated by licence deficiencies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming pay-and-recover for commercial vehicle licence issues. The insurer must pay first.
supporting.quote: it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The principles in Swaran Singh regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach does not extend to all cases. They may try to argue that if the driver never held a licence at all (as opposed to holding a wrong-class or expired licence), this is closer to a 'fake licence' scenario and the insurer should be absolved. However, this case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims, not third-party claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to non-third-party (own-damage) claims. It states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client's claim is a third-party claim under Section 166/163A of the MV Act. The case therefore supports our position by negative implication: Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims, which is exactly what we have.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and pay-and-recover cannot be invoked.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available in all cases. However, this case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire/reward, which is a fundamentally different category from a third-party road user killed by a commercial vehicle.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns passengers carried for hire or reward in a private vehicle — persons who are not 'third parties' under the Act. Our deceased was a pedestrian/other road user (a third party in the classic sense), not a passenger in the offending vehicle. The ratio is expressly limited to non-third-party claimants. The court itself distinguished Shamanna's case (where there was no valid driving licence) as involving a genuine third party where pay-and-recover was proper.
adverse.quote: when the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not a universal remedy. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category expressly excluded from statutory coverage. Our deceased is a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The deceased in our case is a third-party road user (not a gratuitous passenger). Section 147 of the MV Act mandates third-party risk coverage. The risk here IS statutorily required to be covered, unlike gratuitous passengers. The court in this case itself distinguished between risks that are statutorily covered (where pay-and-recover applies) and those that are not (where it does not).
adverse.quote: the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act are not attracted

priority_arguments: Lead with the statutory liability argument: Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act impose an unconditional obligation on the insurer to satisfy third-party awards. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not against the claimant. Cite Satto (doc_033) and Yallavva (doc_025) as primary authorities.

Emphasise that the deceased was a third-party road user, not a passenger in the offending vehicle. The risk to third parties is mandatorily covered under Section 147, and no policy condition can defeat this statutory protection.

Cite Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) as the most factually analogous case: driver with no licence at all, yet pay-and-recover was ordered. This directly refutes the insurer's 'no licence = no liability' argument.

Argue that the insurer's defence under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is available only against the insured, not against the third-party claimant. The breach, even if proved, only entitles the insurer to recover from the owner.

On quantum: the deceased was 42 years old with Rs 35,000 monthly income and 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Apply 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50 per Pranay Sethi), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma), multiplier of 14 (age 42). Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi with 10% triennial enhancement.
If the insurer argues contributory negligence, note that there is no evidence of the deceased's negligence on the facts provided. The burden is on the insurer to prove contributory negligence.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition till realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework: Monthly income Rs 35,000; Annual Rs 4,20,000; Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42) = Rs 5,25,000; Deduct 1/3rd personal expenses (3 dependants) = Rs 3,50,000; Apply multiplier 14 = Rs 49,00,000; Add conventional heads (loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 79,860 + parental consortium Rs 79,860 for 2 minor children) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. If the deceased is treated as permanent employee (30% future prospects), the total would be approximately Rs 52,95,650.
risks: The insurer may argue that a driver who never held a licence constitutes a more serious breach than a driver with an expired or wrong-class licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (doc_032) where the driver had at least an LMV licence. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this scenario and still applies pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the owner of the commercial truck should have verified the driver's licence, and that the owner's failure amounts to a fundamental breach that should absolve the insurer entirely. Counter: the breach is between insurer and insured; the third party is not affected.
Risk of delay: the insurer may appeal any pay-and-recover order, delaying recovery. Consider seeking a direction for the insurer to deposit the amount pending appeal.
If the truck owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer's recovery right may be academic, but this does not affect the claimant's right to be paid first.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek: (a) compensation of approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs with interest; (b) a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the award in the first instance; (c) liberty to the insurer to recover from the owner (pay-and-recover). Alternatively, if the income is well-documented, consider a claim under Section 163A for a speedier remedy, though the structured formula may yield a lower amount than the multiplier method on these facts.

caveats: The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely absolved from paying a third-party claimant solely because the driver had no licence. Every relevant judgment in the corpus applies pay-and-recover. This is consistent with the statutory scheme under Section 149.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific scenario of a driver who never obtained any driving licence at all (as opposed to expired, wrong-class, or fake licence) in the context of a commercial vehicle. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) is the closest analogue and applied pay-and-recover.

The corpus does not contain any judgment from the Supreme Court directly on the 'no licence at all' + 'commercial vehicle' combination. The strongest Supreme Court authority in the corpus is S.Iyyapan (doc_032), which deals with missing endorsement rather than no licence. Counsel should consider citing National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 (not in corpus but binding) which holds that even where the driver has no licence, the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured.

Quantum-related caveat: The computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If the deceased was in permanent employment, future prospects would be 30% (not 25%), increasing the total. Counsel should verify employment status.

The corpus does not contain judgments specifically addressing the quantum of spousal and parental consortium for minor children in the context of a 2026 award. The conventional heads have been computed using the Pranay Sethi framework with 10% triennial enhancement (last enhanced in 2024 per the framework).

payload.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao
payload.holding: The Court held that while an attached trailer/trolley is part of an insured tractor and does not require separate insurance, the insurance company is absolved from liability because the tractor was being used to transport bricks and iron rods for construction rather than for agricultural purposes, violating the insurance policy terms.
payload.ratio: A trailer attached to a tractor is considered part of the tractor and does not require separate insurance under the Motor Vehicles Act; however, if the tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable to pay compensation.

Therefore, it is not required to be insured under the provisions of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and

According to the appellant's counsel, deceased was driving the scooter without holding any valid
license. He also submits that at the time of accident, the tractor was used to transport the bricks and
iron rods for the purpose of construction of Pakki Boring in a room to secure the boring equipments
for irrigation purposes. So, the tractor was used for agricultural purposes. Its driver was having the

valid driving license to drive the tractor and at the time of accident, the tractor was duly insured. So,
the liability will have to be fixed against the insurance company. He relied on the ratio laid down in
the cases of Nagashetty v. United India Insurance Company Ltd.; 2001 A.C.J. 1441; 2001 (3) T.A.C.
511 and also a judgement in the case of Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. J. Kotiratnama, 2000 (3) An.
W.R. 91.
On the other hand, learned counsel for the insurance company submits that the tractor was insured
but trolley was not insured. No premium was paid for the trolley as per Section 61 of the Motor
Vehicles Act, 1988. He further submits that the tractor was insured only for the purpose of
agricultural use but the appellant was carrying the bricks and iron rods in the trolley. So, it is the
violation of the terms and conditions of the policy. Again, he repeated that the trolley is not the part
of the tractor as no premium for the trolley was paid to the insurance company.
We have heard both the parties at length and gone through the material available on record.
There is no dispute regarding the accident or amount of compensation. The only dispute is that who
will pay the compensation i.e. the owner of the tractor or the insurance company.
In the instant case, the tractor in question (No. U.P. 35-B 1649) was duly insured with the insurance
company. Admittedly, no separate premium was paid for the trolley. This was the specific defense
taken by the insurance company.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of National Insurance Company v.

ctor means a motor vehicle which is not itself constructed to
carry any load other than (the equipments used for the purpose) or propulsion but excludes a road
roller.
On a perusal of the definition of word 'tractor' shows that the tractor itself is not able to carry any
load without the equipments. Therefore, any equipments attached to the tractor is a part of the
tractor and covered under the insurance policy.
In view of the above, we observed that the trailer/trolley, which is attached with the tractor is a part
of the tractor, which was duly insured from the insurance company. Hence, the insurance company
cannot escape from its liability to pay compensation by taking the plea that the trailer was not
separately insured.
But in the instant case, fact remains that at the time of accident, the trolley which was attached with
the tractor was carrying the Iron Rods and Bricks for the purpose of construction of a room to cover
the pakki boring as admitted by the appellant in paragraph-3 of the affidavit. Transportation of iron
rods and bricks is certainly not an agricultural activity. The tractor was insured only for the purpose
of agricultural activity. The tractor will have to be used only for agricultural purpose not for any
other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and
conditions of the insurance policy. When it is so, then we are of the view that in the instant case, the
insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to
pay the compensation.
Hence, we uphold the judgment and order dated 27.01.2009 passed by Motor Accident Claims
Tribunal, Unnao in Claim Petition No. 117 of 2001, of course for different reason, as stated above.
Since, the quantum is not disputed, the appellant shall deposit the balance amount, if any, before
the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao within a period of two months. We further direct the
registry to transmit the entire amount to the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao, and the
Tribunal will proceed in terms of the award.

In view of the aforesaid, the appeal is dismissed.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). The accident involved a commercial truck whose driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting and adverse precedents and strategy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: third-party death claim, insurer raised defence of invalid driving licence. The court held the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It establishes that even where the insurer proves a breach (invalid licence), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment. The insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner, not refusal to pay the claimant.
supporting.quote: the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Pursuant to Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision of Karnataka High Court directly holding that even a fundamental breach of policy conditions does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively analyses the statutory scheme. It rejects the argument that a 'fundamental breach' allows the insurer to walk away from third-party liability. The only exception is fraud/collusion, which is not present here.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... or a policy covering other risks

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Most factually analogous: the driver had NO driving licence at all (not expired, not wrong class). The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus. The driver genuinely had no licence. Despite that, the tribunal applied pay-and-recover. It directly refutes the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability to anyone.'
supporting.quote: it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle in the manner provided under law.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (heavy goods vehicle) where driver had LMV licence but no endorsement for HGV. The court applied pay-and-recover. The principle extends to our case where the driver had no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the commercial nature of the vehicle does not change the pay-and-recover principle. The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be contracted away.
supporting.quote: the insurer would remain liable to the innocent third party, but it may be able to recover from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required, there is a breach but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial/transport vehicle, driver lacked proper licence class. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that licence deficiency does not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming that even for transport/commercial vehicles, the pay-and-recover principle applies. The insurer cannot refuse to pay the third party.
supporting.quote: the Insurance Company must first pay the compensation amount to the claimant and then recover the same from the insured owner due to breach of policy conditions regarding the driver's license.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle while possessing a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 overrides policy conditions about licence endorsements.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court precedent that the insurer's obligation to third parties is statutory and cannot be defeated by technical licence deficiencies. While this case involved a driver who had some licence (unlike our facts), the ratio on the primacy of third-party protection is binding.
supporting.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case where the court held the insurer must pay the third party. The ratio extends to any licence deficiency.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the licence is not valid on the date of accident, the third-party claim is not defeated. The insurer's remedy is against the insured.
supporting.quote: the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover, but the third party must still be paid.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (tanker) where driver lacked special endorsement for hazardous goods. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that third-party claims are not defeated by licence deficiencies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming pay-and-recover for commercial vehicle licence issues. The insurer must pay first.
supporting.quote: it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it does not cover the interregnum period, but the insurer must still satisfy the award and recover from the insured under pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Lapsed licence case where the court held the driver did not have a valid licence on the accident date, but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the licence is definitively invalid on the accident date, the third-party claimant is still protected by pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: the liability fastened on the Insurance Company to pay the compensation and recover the same from the owner of the vehicle

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The principles in Swaran Singh regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach does not extend to all cases. They may try to argue that if the driver never held a licence at all (as opposed to holding a wrong-class or expired licence), this is closer to a 'fake licence' scenario and the insurer should be absolved. However, this case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims, not third-party claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to non-third-party (own-damage) claims. It states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client's claim is a third-party claim under Section 166 of the MV Act. The case therefore supports our position by negative implication: Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims, which is exactly what we have.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence can be inferred from the fact that the injured person was driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet, leading to a 50% deduction in compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if the deceased was himself driving a vehicle without a licence (if that were the case), contributory negligence should reduce compensation. However, on the facts provided, the deceased was a pedestrian/occupant of another vehicle killed by a commercial truck — not driving himself. The risk is that the Tribunal might entertain a contributory negligence argument on other grounds (e.g., the deceased suddenly crossed the road).
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about an injured motorcyclist who was himself driving without a licence and without a helmet — his own negligence contributed to his injuries. In our case, the deceased was not driving the offending vehicle; he was a third-party road user. The absence of the truck driver's licence goes to the insurer's defence under Section 149(2), not to the deceased's conduct. There is no evidence of contributory negligence by the deceased on the facts provided.
adverse.quote: he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger is travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such a passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and pay-and-recover cannot be invoked.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available in all cases and that the court has no inherent power to order it. However, this case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire/reward, which is a fundamentally different category from a third-party road user killed by a commercial vehicle.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns passengers carried for hire or reward in a private vehicle — persons who are not 'third parties' under the Act. Our deceased was a third-party road user (not a passenger in the offending vehicle). The court itself distinguished Shamanna's case (where there was no valid driving licence) as involving a genuine third party where pay-and-recover was proper. The ratio is expressly limited to non-third-party claimants.
adverse.quote: when the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as 'third party'; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover'

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not a universal remedy and that the court's power is limited. However, this case is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category expressly excluded from statutory coverage. Our deceased is a third-party road user, whose risk is mandatorily covered under Section 147.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The deceased in our case is a third-party road user (not a gratuitous passenger). Section 147 of the MV Act mandates third-party risk coverage. The risk here IS statutorily required to be covered, unlike gratuitous passengers. The court in this case itself distinguished between risks that are statutorily covered (where pay-and-recover applies) and those that are not (where it does not).
adverse.quote: the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act are not attracted

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Ellappa ... 1St
adverse.principle: The insurance company has no statutory liability to pay compensation to passengers travelling in a goods vehicle, though appellate courts retain discretion to apply pay-and-recover depending on facts.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is discretionary, not automatic. However, this case concerns passengers in goods vehicles (not third parties), and the court still applied pay-and-recover in favour of the claimants. The risk is low because our deceased is a third-party road user, not a passenger.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns passengers travelling in a goods vehicle — persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased is a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered under Section 147. The court in Ellappa itself acknowledged that where the insurer is successful in its defence under Section 149(2), it 'may yet be required to pay the amount to the claimant and thereafter recover the same from the owner' — which is exactly our situation.
adverse.quote: Where the Insurance Company is successful in its defence, it may yet be required to pay the amount to the claimant and thereafter recover the same from the owner under such circumstance envisaged and enumerated in Section 149(4) and Section 149(5).

adverse.title: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
adverse.principle: A person travelling on the mud-guard of a tractor is not covered by statutory insurance, and pay-and-recover cannot be granted when the travel violates safety regulations.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available where the claimant is not a 'third party' within the meaning of the Act. However, this case concerns a person sitting on a tractor mud-guard — an inherently dangerous and prohibited position. Our deceased is a standard third-party road user.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The claimant in this case was sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor — a position expressly prohibited by Regulation 28 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicle Regulations. The court held such a person 'cannot claim to be a third party.' Our deceased was a third-party road user in the classic sense — not a passenger on the offending vehicle in any prohibited position. The benefit of pay-and-recover is a statutory right of a genuine third party.
adverse.quote: the claimant by sitting over mud-guard of tractor engine, cannot claim to be a third party. Therefore, for the persons who are not third parties, benefit of pay and recovery cannot be given.

priority_arguments: Lead with the statutory liability argument: Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act impose an unconditional obligation on the insurer to satisfy third-party awards. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not against the claimant. Cite Satto (doc_033) and Yallavva (doc_025) as primary authorities.

Emphasise that the deceased was a third-party road user, not a passenger in the offending vehicle. The risk to third parties is mandatorily covered under Section 147, and no policy condition can defeat this statutory protection.

Cite Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) as the most factually analogous case: driver with no licence at all, yet pay-and-recover was ordered. This directly refutes the insurer's 'no licence = no liability' argument.

Argue that the insurer's defence under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is available only against the insured, not against the third-party claimant. The breach, even if proved, only entitles the insurer to recover from the owner.

On quantum: the deceased was 42 years old with Rs 35,000 monthly income and 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Apply 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50 per Pranay Sethi), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma), multiplier of 14 (age 42). Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi with 10% triennial enhancement.

If the insurer argues contributory negligence, note that there is no evidence of the deceased's negligence on the facts provided. The burden is on the insurer to prove contributory negligence. The deceased's status as a third-party road user (not a driver) makes a contributory negligence defence unlikely to succeed.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition till realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework: Monthly income Rs 35,000; Annual Rs 4,20,000; Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42) = Rs 5,25,000; Deduct 1/3rd personal expenses (3 dependants) = Rs 3,50,000; Apply multiplier 14 = Rs 49,00,000; Add conventional heads (loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 79,860 + parental consortium Rs 79,860 for 2 minor children) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. If the deceased is treated as permanent employee (30% future prospects), the total would be approximately Rs 52,95,650.
risks: The insurer may argue that a driver who never held a licence constitutes a more serious breach than a driver with an expired or wrong-class licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (doc_032) where the driver had at least an LMV licence. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this scenario and still applies pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the owner of the commercial truck should have verified the driver's licence, and that the owner's failure amounts to a fundamental breach that should absolve the insurer entirely. Counter: the breach is between insurer and insured; the third party is not affected.
Risk of delay: the insurer may appeal any pay-and-recover order, delaying recovery. Consider seeking a direction for the insurer to deposit the amount pending appeal.
If the truck owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer's recovery right may be academic, but this does not affect the claimant's right to be paid first.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek: (a) compensation of approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs with interest; (b) a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the award in the first instance; (c) liberty to the insurer to recover from the owner (pay-and-recover). Alternatively, if the income is well-documented, consider a claim under Section 163A for a speedier remedy, though the structured formula may yield a lower amount than the multiplier method on these facts.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi) — Irrelevant. Concerns a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes in breach of policy terms about vehicle use, not about driver licence. The insurer was absolved because the vehicle was used for a purpose not covered by the policy at all. No bearing on our case where the breach is about driver licence, not vehicle use.

doc_007 (National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.) — Irrelevant. Concerns whether a non-dependent legal representative can claim loss of dependency. A quantum/entitlement issue, not about insurer liability for licence breach. Does not affect our case where all three dependants (wife + 2 minor children) are clearly dependent.

doc_014 (Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.) — Irrelevant. Concerns gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (tractor). The deceased was a passenger, not a third-party road user. The insurer was absolved because the risk was not statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased is a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered.

doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P) — Irrelevant. A criminal revision concerning rash driving conviction under IPC. The court set aside the conviction for rash driving but upheld the fine under Section 181 MV Act for driving without a licence. This is a criminal matter with no bearing on civil compensation liability.

doc_038 (M/S Crown Consultants (P) Ltd. vs The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.) — Irrelevant. A consumer dispute about repudiation of a stockbroker's fidelity insurance claim for late filing. Entirely different area of law (insurance contract, not motor accident).
doc_051 (Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State) — Irrelevant. Criminal proceedings for quashing of FIR in economic fraud. No connection to motor accident law.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy vs K.Viswanathan) — Irrelevant. Civil suit for specific performance of a sale agreement. No connection to motor accident or insurance law.

The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely absolved from paying a third-party claimant solely because the driver had no licence. Every relevant judgment in the corpus applies pay-and-recover. This is consistent with the statutory scheme under Section 149.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific scenario of a driver who never obtained any driving licence at all (as opposed to expired, wrong-class, or fake licence) in the context of a commercial vehicle. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) is the closest analogue and applied pay-and-recover.

The corpus does not contain any judgment from the Supreme Court directly on the 'no licence at all' + 'commercial vehicle' combination. The strongest Supreme Court authority in the corpus is S.Iyyapan (doc_032), which deals with missing endorsement rather than no licence. Counsel should consider citing National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 (not in corpus but binding) which holds that even where the driver has no licence, the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured.

Quantum-related caveat: The computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If the deceased was in permanent employment, future prospects would be 30% (not 25%), increasing the total. Counsel should verify employment status.

The corpus does not contain judgments specifically addressing the quantum of spousal and parental consortium for minor children in the context of a 2026 award. The conventional heads have been computed using the Pranay Sethi framework with 10% triennial enhancement (last enhanced in 2024 per the framework).

payload.holding: The appeal of the insurance company is dismissed, and the appeal of the claimants is partly allowed by setting aside the finding of contributory negligence, factoring in future prospects, and enhancing the total compensation to Rs. 13,74,876/- with a pay-and-recover order against the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Where there is consistent and unimpeached oral testimony of an eye-witness establishing the absence of negligence on the part of the deceased, a tribunal cannot record a finding of contributory negligence merely by drawing assumptions from a police sketch or site plan that does not conclusively indicate a head-on collision. Furthermore, even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi (widow) for death of her husband aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, with two minor children (8 and 12). The accident involved a commercial truck whose driver had no valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing the policy is void due to unlicensed driver. Research supporting and adverse precedents and strategy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: third-party death claim, insurer raised defence of invalid driving licence. The court held the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent. It establishes that even where the insurer proves a breach (invalid licence), the third-party claimant is still entitled to payment. The insurer's remedy is recovery from the owner, not refusal to pay the claimant.
supporting.quote: the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be, as ordered by the Claims Tribunal or the Court.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Pursuant to Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision of Karnataka High Court directly holding that even a fundamental breach of policy conditions does not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively analyses the statutory scheme. It rejects the argument that a 'fundamental breach' allows the insurer to walk away from third-party liability. The only exception is fraud/collusion, which is not present here.
supporting.quote: the insurer or Insurance Company is liable to satisfy the award vis-à-vis a third party and is entitled to recover from the insured. This is irrespective of, the policy being an Act policy... or a policy covering other risks

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Most factually analogous: the driver had NO driving licence at all (not expired, not wrong class). The tribunal held it was a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the closest factual match in the corpus. The driver genuinely had no licence. Despite that, the tribunal applied pay-and-recover. It directly refutes the insurer's argument that 'no licence = no liability to anyone.'
supporting.quote: it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle in the manner provided under law.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner. The insurer's appeal against pay-and-recover was dismissed.
supporting.fact_alignment: The insurer argued that because the driver had no valid licence, it could not be forced to pay. The High Court rejected this argument, applied pay-and-recover, and dismissed the insurer's appeal. Directly supports our position.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a High Court judgment that specifically considered and rejected the exact argument National Insurance Co. is making here — that no valid licence means no liability. The court held that S.Iyyapan (Supreme Court) governs and pay-and-recover applies.
supporting.quote: even if the offending vehicle was being driven by the driver having no valid driving license, insurer is liable to pay compensation to the claimants and further insurer has a right to recover the amount of compensation from the insured i.e. owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (heavy goods vehicle) where driver had LMV licence but no endorsement for HGV. The court applied pay-and-recover. The principle extends to our case where the driver had no licence at all.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the commercial nature of the vehicle does not change the pay-and-recover principle. The insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and cannot be contracted away.
supporting.quote: the insurer would remain liable to the innocent third party, but it may be able to recover from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation required, there is a breach but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial/transport vehicle, driver lacked proper licence class. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that licence deficiency does not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming that even for transport/commercial vehicles, the pay-and-recover principle applies. The insurer cannot refuse to pay the third party.
supporting.quote: the Insurance Company must first pay the compensation amount to the claimant and then recover the same from the insured owner due to breach of policy conditions regarding the driver's license.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle while possessing a valid LMV licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Supreme Court authority that the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 overrides policy conditions about licence endorsements.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supreme Court precedent that the insurer's obligation to third parties is statutory and cannot be defeated by technical licence deficiencies. While this case involved a driver who had some licence (unlike our facts), the ratio on the primacy of third-party protection is binding.
supporting.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: Expired licence case where the court held the insurer must pay the third party. The ratio extends to any licence deficiency.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even where the licence is not valid on the date of accident, the third-party claim is not defeated. The insurer's remedy is against the insured.
supporting.quote: the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award passed against the third party and the conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement on the driving licence constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover, but the third party must still be paid.
supporting.fact_alignment: Commercial vehicle (tanker) where driver lacked special endorsement for hazardous goods. Pay-and-recover ordered. Supports the principle that third-party claims are not defeated by licence deficiencies.
supporting.why_it_matters: Another precedent confirming pay-and-recover for commercial vehicle licence issues. The insurer must pay first.
supporting.quote: it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount of compensation awarded by the Tribunal from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it does not cover the interregnum period, but the insurer must still satisfy the award and recover from the insured under pay-and-recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Lapsed licence case where the court held the driver did not have a valid licence on the accident date, but still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the licence is definitively invalid on the accident date, the third-party claimant is still protected by pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: the liability fastened on the Insurance Company to pay the compensation and recover the same from the owner of the vehicle

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The principles in Swaran Singh regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach does not extend to all cases. They may try to argue that if the driver never held a licence at all, this is closer to a 'fake licence' scenario and the insurer should be absolved. However, this case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims, not third-party claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Laxmi Narain Dhut expressly limits its holding to non-third-party (own-damage) claims. It states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client's claim is a third-party claim under Section 166 of the MV Act. The case therefore supports our position by negative implication: Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims, which is exactly what we have. Additionally, doc_006 (Meena) in this corpus specifically considered and rejected the argument that Sujata Arora/Laxmi Narain Dhut line of cases applies to third-party claims, holding instead that S.Iyyapan governs.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Contributory negligence can be inferred from the fact that the injured person was driving without a valid driving licence and without wearing a helmet, leading to a 50% deduction in compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that if the deceased was himself driving a vehicle without a licence (if that were the case), contributory negligence should reduce compensation. However, on the facts provided, the deceased was a third-party road user killed by a commercial truck — not driving himself. The risk is that the Tribunal might entertain a contributory negligence argument on other grounds (e.g., the deceased suddenly crossed the road).
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about an injured motorcyclist who was himself driving without a licence and without a helmet — his own negligence contributed to his injuries. In our case, the deceased was not driving the offending vehicle; he was a third-party road user. The absence of the truck driver's licence goes to the insurer's defence under Section 149(2), not to the deceased's conduct. There is no evidence of contributory negligence by the deceased on the facts provided.
adverse.quote: he did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50 % of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

priority_arguments: Lead with the statutory liability argument: Section 149(1) and (4) of the MV Act impose an unconditional obligation on the insurer to satisfy third-party awards. The insurer's remedy is against the insured, not against the claimant. Cite Satto (doc_033) and Yallavva (doc_025) as primary authorities.

Emphasise that the deceased was a third-party road user, not a passenger in the offending vehicle. The risk to third parties is mandatorily covered under Section 147, and no policy condition can defeat this statutory protection.

Cite Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) as the most factually analogous case: driver with no licence at all, yet pay-and-recover was ordered. This directly refutes the insurer's 'no licence = no liability' argument.

Cite Meena (doc_006) where the High Court specifically rejected the insurer's argument that no valid licence means no liability, and applied pay-and-recover citing S.Iyyapan. This judgment directly addresses and defeats the insurer's likely line of argument.

Argue that the insurer's defence under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) is available only against the insured, not against the third-party claimant. The breach, even if proved, only entitles the insurer to recover from the owner.

On quantum: the deceased was 42 years old with Rs 35,000 monthly income and 3 dependants (wife + 2 minor children). Apply 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 40-50 per Pranay Sethi), 1/3rd deduction for personal expenses (3 dependants per Sarla Verma), multiplier of 14 (age 42). Conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi with 10% triennial enhancement.

If the insurer argues contributory negligence, note that there is no evidence of the deceased's negligence on the facts provided. The burden is on the insurer to prove contributory negligence. The deceased's status as a third-party road user (not a driver) makes a contributory negligence defence unlikely to succeed.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition till realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework: Monthly income Rs 35,000; Annual Rs 4,20,000; Add 25% future prospects (self-employed, age 42) = Rs 5,25,000; Deduct 1/3rd personal expenses (3 dependants) = Rs 3,50,000; Apply multiplier 14 = Rs 49,00,000; Add conventional heads (loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 79,860 + parental consortium Rs 79,860 for 2 minor children) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. If the deceased is treated as permanent employee (30% future prospects), the total would be approximately Rs 52,95,650.
risks: The insurer may argue that a driver who never held a licence constitutes a more serious breach than a driver with an expired or wrong-class licence, and may seek to distinguish cases like S.Iyyapan (doc_032) where the driver had at least an LMV licence. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) directly addresses this scenario and still applies pay-and-recover.

The insurer may argue that the owner of the commercial truck should have verified the driver's licence, and that the owner's failure amounts to a fundamental breach that should absolve the insurer entirely. Counter: the breach is between insurer and insured; the third party is not affected.
Risk of delay: the insurer may appeal any pay-and-recover order, delaying recovery. Consider seeking a direction for the insurer to deposit the amount pending appeal.
If the truck owner is impecunious or untraceable, the insurer's recovery right may be academic, but this does not affect the claimant's right to be paid first.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim petition under Section 166 of the MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek: (a) compensation of approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs with interest; (b) a declaration that the insurer is liable to pay the award in the first instance; (c) liberty to the insurer to recover from the owner (pay-and-recover). Alternatively, if the income is well-documented, consider a claim under Section 163A for a speedier remedy, though the structured formula may yield a lower amount than the multiplier method on these facts.

caveats: doc_002 (Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi) — Irrelevant. Concerns a tractor used for non-agricultural purposes in breach of policy terms about vehicle use, not about driver licence. The insurer was absolved because the vehicle was used for a purpose not covered by the policy at all. No bearing on our case where the breach is about driver licence, not vehicle use.

doc_007 (National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.) — Irrelevant. Concerns whether a non-dependent legal representative can claim loss of dependency. A quantum/entitlement issue, not about insurer liability for licence breach. Does not affect our case where all three dependants (wife + 2 minor children) are clearly dependent.

doc_014 (Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.) — Irrelevant. Concerns gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (tractor). The deceased was a passenger, not a third-party road user. The insurer was absolved because the risk was not statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased is a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered.

doc_016 (Reserved On: 21.07.2025 vs State Of H.P) — Irrelevant. A criminal revision concerning rash driving conviction under IPC. The court set aside the conviction for rash driving but upheld the fine under Section 181 MV Act for driving without a licence. This is a criminal matter with no bearing on civil compensation liability.

doc_026 (National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Ellappa) — Irrelevant. Concerns passengers travelling in a goods vehicle — persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered. Our deceased is a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered under Section 147. The court in Ellappa itself acknowledged that where the insurer is successful in its defence under Section 149(2), it may still be required to pay and recover — which supports our position.

doc_028 (United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam) — Irrelevant. Concerns passengers in a private vehicle for hire/reward — persons who are not 'third parties' under the Act. Our deceased is a third-party road user. The court itself distinguished Shamanna's case (no valid driving licence) as involving a genuine third party where pay-and-recover was proper.

doc_029 (United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai) — Irrelevant. Concerns gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — a category expressly excluded from statutory coverage. Our deceased is a third-party road user whose risk IS statutorily covered under Section 147.

doc_030 (Dadapeera vs Mallesh) — Irrelevant. Concerns a person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor — an inherently dangerous and prohibited position. The court held such a person 'cannot claim to be a third party.' Our deceased is a third-party road user in the classic sense.

doc_038 (M/S Crown Consultants (P) Ltd. vs The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.) — Irrelevant. A consumer dispute about repudiation of a stockbroker's fidelity insurance claim for late filing. Entirely different area of law (insurance contract, not motor accident).
doc_051 (Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State) — Irrelevant. Criminal proceedings for quashing of FIR in economic fraud. No connection to motor accident law.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy vs K.Viswanathan) — Irrelevant. Civil suit for specific performance of a sale agreement. No connection to motor accident or insurance law.

The corpus does not contain any judgment where the insurer was completely absolved from paying a third-party claimant solely because the driver had no licence. Every relevant judgment in the corpus applies pay-and-recover. This is consistent with the statutory scheme under Section 149.

No judgment in the corpus addresses the specific scenario of a driver who never obtained any driving licence at all (as opposed to expired, wrong-class, or fake licence) in the context of a commercial vehicle. However, Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) is the closest analogue and applied pay-and-recover.

The corpus does not contain any judgment from the Supreme Court directly on the 'no licence at all' + 'commercial vehicle' combination. The strongest Supreme Court authority in the corpus is S.Iyyapan (doc_032), which deals with missing endorsement rather than no licence. Counsel should consider citing National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 (not in corpus but binding) which holds that even where the driver has no licence, the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured.

Quantum-related caveat: The computation assumes the deceased was self-employed. If the deceased was in permanent employment, future prospects would be 30% (not 25%), increasing the total. Counsel should verify employment status.

The corpus does not contain judgments specifically addressing the quantum of spousal and parental consortium for minor children in the context of a 2026 award. The conventional heads have been computed using the Pranay Sethi framework with 10% triennial enhancement (last enhanced in 2024 per the framework).
